passage: Note from Avni, school counsellor. At Thursday's parent meeting, Jomon sat with his son Rohit's report and said, more than once, "The neighbour's boy already has a rank in the top ten. Why can't he do the same?" His jaw was tight, and he kept turning his pen. When I asked what he was hoping for, he said, "I wanted to study engineering and never could. I don't want Rohit to end up behind like me." He looked surprised at his own words. I asked what Rohit hears when he says it. After a pause, Jomon said, "Probably that he isn't enough." What I did: I suggested he name one thing Rohit really worked at, and he mentioned the neat maths notebook Rohit had kept up for a month. He wrote it down to say at home.

qa.q: What did Jomon say the neighbour's boy already had?
qa.a: He said the neighbour's boy already had a rank in the top ten.

qa.q: What was Jomon afraid of when he compared Rohit to the neighbour's boy?
qa.a: He was afraid Rohit would fall behind as he felt he had, and his own regret over engineering sat under the comparison.

qa.q: What could Jomon do at home that would motivate Rohit better than comparing?
qa.a: He could praise real effort, such as the neat maths notebook, so Rohit knows his father sees the work he does.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel hearing his father's comparison?
qa.a: Probably that he isn't enough, as Jomon himself guessed, which could make love feel conditional on results.

grounding: Shows a parent comparing his child from fear and regret, seen by a counsellor who helps him notice and praise real effort.

passage:
Dear Anjali,

At Nani's on Sunday, when Aunty said, "Why can't you be like Elizabeth?" I saw your face close, and I've felt bad ever since. I couldn't say anything in front of everyone.

So I'm saying it here. I'm not the perfect cousin they think I am. I nearly failed the physics test in November, and I cry in the bathroom before some exams. I hate being held up like a trophy, because then I can't tell anybody when things are hard.

Can we get chai this week, just us? I promise no marks talk, and I won't gloat. ❤️

Elizabeth

qa.q: Which subject did Elizabeth nearly fail in November?
qa.a: She nearly failed the physics test.

qa.q: What is Elizabeth feeling about being held up as the ideal cousin?
qa.a: She feels awkward and uncomfortable, unable to admit her own struggles because she is on a pedestal.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do to keep the friendship with Anjali steady?
qa.a: She can stay kind, be honest about her own difficulties and avoid gloating, as she does in the letter by inviting Anjali for chai. ❤️

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when the aunt compares her to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Probably small and stung, which is why her face closed, and she may be envious without disliking Elizabeth herself.

grounding: Shows a teen cousin held up as ideal who writes kindly, admits her own difficulties and refuses to gloat.

passage:
Sunday. At lunch Harsha's father said, "Your cousin got into the science stream with a scholarship. Take a lesson." Harsha kept chewing. "Okay." Inside, he told himself he didn't care.

Thursday. His maths homework sat unopened for three days. When his friend asked, he shrugged. "Why bother?" He noticed the flatness: no anger, no shame, just a grey nothing where those used to be.

The following Saturday. In the kitchen, he asked himself: Do I not care, or have I just stopped feeling it? He suspected the second. He told his mother Gargi, quietly, "I stopped listening when Papa compares me. I think it still hurts." She put the ladle down and said, "Then tell me what it feels like."

qa.q: What did Harsha's father say his cousin got into?
qa.a: He said his cousin got into the science stream with a scholarship.

qa.q: What did Harsha suspect about his flat feeling by the following Saturday?
qa.a: He suspected he hadn't stopped caring but had stopped feeling, because the hurt was still there under the grey nothing.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next to avoid shutting down his effort altogether?
qa.a: He can keep the honest talk with Gargi going and go back to his homework, since numbness protects him only in the short term.

qa.q: How might Harsha's mother see his shrug at first?
qa.a: Possibly as not caring, which is why hearing that it still hurts probably surprised her and made her put down the ladle.

grounding: Shows a teen who goes numb to comparisons and tells himself he does not care, then notices it and has one honest talk.

passage:
Saturday, 10 pm.

Dad moved out today. His bags were by the door at nine and the car left before lunch. Mum kept saying "we're all fine" in a bright voice. I said I was fine too. I wasn't. I went to the bathroom, turned on the tap and cried until my head ached.

Still set my alarm. Still did homework. It helps to have things that stay the same.

Told Vandana at lunch. She didn't say anything smart, just sat next to me on the steps and let me cry a bit more. She's going to come over tomorrow.

I keep thinking of our old Sundays. I miss a family that turns out not to have been there. It's my loss too.

Payal

qa.q: What time were Dad's bags by the door?
qa.a: His bags were by the door at nine.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she said she was fine and then went to the bathroom to cry?
qa.a: She was grieving and sad, and she said she was fine to match her mum's bright voice.

qa.q: What did Payal do that helps her cope?
qa.a: She let herself cry, kept her alarm and homework routine, and told her friend Vandana how she felt.

qa.q: How did Vandana's way of responding help Payal?
qa.a: She didn't try to say anything clever. She sat beside Payal and let her cry, which made Payal feel that her sadness was allowed. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teen mourning the family she thought she had, letting herself cry, keeping routines and confiding in a friend.

passage:
Saturday. When Uday came to collect his last boxes, Pallavi went to her room and shut the door. She heard him ask her mother, "Is she still not talking to me?" She turned her music louder. It was his fault. She had decided that.

The following Friday. Her grandmother found her staring at a photo of the three of them at the beach. "You're angry." "Yes." "Anger is often sadness wearing armour, and grown-up marriages are more tangled than they look from outside." Pallavi said nothing, but she didn't put the photo away.

The Sunday after. Uday knocked. She opened the door. "I'm not ready to talk about it," she said. "But you can ask me about my exam." He sat on the bed's far end and asked. She answered, and it was the first time in weeks she hadn't left the room.

qa.q: What was Pallavi looking at when her grandmother found her?
qa.a: She was staring at a photo of the three of them at the beach.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel toward her father on the first Saturday, and what might lie under it?
qa.a: She felt angry and blamed him, and her grandmother suggested the anger could be covering sadness.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do on the last Sunday that kept the door open without forcing things?
qa.a: She said she wasn't ready to talk about the divorce but let him ask about her exam, staying in the room with him.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt when he stood outside his daughter's shut door?
qa.a: Probably hurt and worried about losing her, since he asked her mother about her and later came back and knocked again.

grounding: Shows a teen blaming a parent and leaving the room, then recognising the sadness under the anger and letting the parent back in slowly.

passage: By the time the sun climbed over the wheat, Kamal had swept the yard, fed the buffaloes and finished two chapters of homework. His mother Rukmini watched him from the doorway, holding her tea. "You're up early. Again." "Just helping, Ma." He kept sweeping. All week he had been doing this. Under it sat a small hard thought: if he hadn't argued so much with his brother, if he had scored better in maths, maybe his parents wouldn't be splitting up. Rukmini set down her tea and sat on the step. "Kamal, come here. Your father and I have talked. Nothing you did caused this. Nothing." His broom slowed. His shoulders shook. "You can love us both, and you don't have to be perfect for us."

qa.q: What had Kamal finished before sunrise?
qa.a: He had swept the yard, fed the buffaloes and finished two chapters of homework.

qa.q: What secret thought was Kamal carrying under all his chores?
qa.a: He wondered whether his arguments with his brother or his maths marks had caused his parents' split, which made him try to be perfect.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do that helped Kamal, and what could he do next?
qa.a: She told him plainly that nothing he did caused it. He can keep loving both parents and let the chores go back to normal, instead of trying to fix them by behaving perfectly.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel seeing her son work so hard all week?
qa.a: Probably worried and sad, since the extra chores told her Kamal was carrying something heavy, and she chose to answer it with plain, clear words.

grounding: Shows a teen secretly wondering if his fights or grades caused his parents' split, trying to be perfect, and hearing plainly that it was not his fault.

passage: I'm Bidisha, and for a while after Baba moved out, my mother Lakshmi started using me as a go-between. "Tell your father the money is late again." "Ask him who lives in that flat with him." At night she'd say things like, "He never cared about us. You see that, don't you?" I felt sick every time, as if I had to pick a side and carry the messages between them. One evening I said, as gently as I could, "Ma, I love you both. I can't carry messages or report on Baba. You can call him yourself." She went quiet and cross. When it kept happening, I told my aunt at school, who is our counsellor, and she helped me find words to say it again, kindly but clearly.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi tell Bidisha to ask about the flat?
qa.a: She told her to ask him who lived in that flat with him.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when her mother asked her to carry messages and agree that her father never cared?
qa.a: She felt sick and pulled between them, as if she had to choose a side.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do to handle the pressure?
qa.a: She kindly refused to carry messages or report, said she loves both, and told a trusted adult when it continued. 🤍

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have been feeling when she asked Bidisha to carry messages?
qa.a: Likely hurt, angry and lonely herself, which does not make it Bidisha's job, and which may be why she went quiet and cross when refused.

grounding: Shows a teen used as messenger and spy by a parent who badmouths the other, kindly refusing and telling a trusted adult.

passage: Note from Anjali, school counsellor. Elizabeth, Class 9, came to see me after her mother and father each asked her, on the same weekend, what the other had said and done. She told me she had a lovely Sunday with her father and kept quiet about it at home, because her mother's face went hard when his name came up. "If I say I miss him, I'm betraying her. If I say I'm fine at home, I'm betraying him." Her hands were pulled into her sleeves. I noticed she seemed less afraid when she said, "I love them both." What I did: we practised a short line she can use with each parent, and she chose, "I love you both and I'm not going to choose."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth keep quiet about at home?
qa.a: She kept quiet about having a lovely Sunday with her father.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth afraid of when she thought about telling either parent that she missed the other?
qa.a: She feared that loving one parent would betray the other, so she hid her affection to keep the peace.

qa.q: What did Anjali do to help Elizabeth respond to her parents?
qa.a: She helped her practise a short honest line, "I love you both and I'm not going to choose," which she can use with each parent.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's mother feel if Elizabeth spoke warmly about her father at home?
qa.a: Probably hurt and afraid of being left out, as her hard face suggests, but Elizabeth's line can reassure her without picking a side.

grounding: Shows a teen torn about loving both divorcing parents, hiding affection to keep peace, and choosing to say she loves both.

passage: Simran, last Saturday you said, "Mum is impatient, Papa forgets things, and they're better apart. I have my own exams." I noticed you weren't angry when you said it, and I was glad. I'm Rekha, your Nani, and I'll tell you about my own parents, who separated when I was sixteen. I was calm very quickly. Too quickly. I told everyone I understood, and by nineteen it all crashed out in a college hostel corridor, over nothing. What I learnt was that calm needs some crying before it. You seem to have done yours. Keep visiting both houses, and tell them honestly how you are. And if the sadness returns, let it. It doesn't mean you took a step back.

qa.q: How old was Rekha when her parents separated?
qa.a: She was sixteen.

qa.q: What does Simran's calm remark about her parents suggest about how she now sees them?
qa.a: She seems to see them as imperfect people who do better apart and to focus on her own life, without anger.

qa.q: What advice does Rekha give Simran about handling her family from here?
qa.a: To keep visiting both houses, be honest with each parent about how she feels, and let sadness come back if it does.

qa.q: How does Rekha's own story differ from Simran's situation?
qa.a: Rekha became calm too quickly without grieving and it crashed out at nineteen, while Simran seems to have cried first, so her calm looks steadier.

grounding: Shows a teen who has come to see both divorcing parents as flawed people better apart, with an elder warning against forcing calm before grieving.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal Mama,

I'm writing because I don't know how to say this on the phone. Since the separation, Mummy sleeps very late and often forgets things. Last Tuesday there was no dinner, and I had cereal. She forgot to sign my exam form, and the last date is Friday. I'm not blaming her. I think she's sad and tired, and it isn't because of me.

Could you help me with the exam form on Wednesday? And could I have dinner at your house two evenings a week for now? I'll get myself there after school.

I'd also like someone to ask how I'm doing. Sometimes I feel forgotten.

Thank you,
Parveen

qa.q: Which day is the last date for the exam form?
qa.a: The last date is Friday.

qa.q: What is Parveen feeling about her mother's forgetfulness?
qa.a: She feels hurt and sometimes forgotten, though she does not blame her mother and thinks she is sad and tired.

qa.q: What is Parveen doing that could help her get what she needs?
qa.a: She is asking clearly for help with the form, regular dinners and someone to ask how she is, and she is turning to a relative.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal Mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably worried and touched that Parveen trusted him, and eager to help her and check on his sister as well.

grounding: Shows a teen whose parent is absorbed in pain and forgets meals and exam forms, asking a relative clearly for what she needs.
